analysis.one_liner: Opens vast public lands and waters to oil, gas, and oil shale leasing, builds nuclear plants and coal-to-liquid fuel, and pays for new renewable power with drilling revenue.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2010 with 8 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to six House committees and five subcommittees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced three months after the Deepwater Horizon spill, would have declared a draft offshore drilling plan legally approved and environmentally compliant, required lease sales every 270 days in areas with commercial interest, opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas leasing, opened more federal land to oil shale, had the Pentagon build a coal-to-liquids fuel plant, and ordered the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue permits for 200 new nuclear reactors by 2040. It would have limited environmental reviews for much of this activity and fast-tracked court challenges. New drilling and oil shale revenue would have gone into a fund paying bonuses to renewable energy producers through competitive auctions.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and oil shale companies get more federal acreage offered for lease, faster sales, weakened environmental review, easier court challenges to overcome, and the option to satisfy mitigation requirements by paying for projects far from the damage. The nuclear industry gets a statutory mandate for 200 reactor permits and a revived Yucca Mountain waste repository. Coal producers get a Defense Department coal-to-liquids facility and repeal of a law limiting federal purchases of high-carbon alternative fuels. Renewable energy producers get auction-funded bonuses, but only from fossil-fuel revenue that depends on the expanded drilling succeeding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, oil shale, nuclear, and coal companies

how_it_helps.text: Declares the draft 2010-2015 offshore leasing plan legally approved and in full compliance with environmental laws, and requires a lease sale every 270 days in each offshore planning region with commercial interest.

Requires each five-year offshore leasing program to offer at least 75% of available unleased acreage in each planning area, and repeals the legal ban on oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, with the first Coastal Plain lease sale within 22 months of enactment.

Cuts environmental review: offshore seismic work and lease suspensions are categorically excluded from environmental assessment, one program-wide environmental impact statement covers all lease sales under it, and exploration plans need no environmental impact statement.

Directs the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue operating permits for 200 new commercial nuclear reactors by 2040, continue the Yucca Mountain waste repository license review, and set up licensing for spent-fuel recycling.
Directs the Secretary of Defense to build and operate a coal-to-liquids facility and repeals the federal restriction on procuring alternative fuels based on their lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions.

Creates an American-Made Energy Trust Fund from new offshore and oil shale lease revenues, and directs the Department of Energy to run reverse auctions awarding those funds to renewable electricity generators, with 25% of each auction reserved for small facilities and 25% for mid-sized ones.
Sends 50% of federal revenues from Arctic Refuge leasing to the State of Alaska, and creates a small (capped at $11 million) impact-aid fund for Alaska communities near the Coastal Plain.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the public inherit the environmental and fiscal costs: the Pentagon must fund a coal-to-liquids plant subject to appropriations; federal environmental review is curtailed or waived for offshore leasing, exploration, and Arctic Refuge development; and legal challenges are limited to a 60-day window in one D.C. court with the government's environmental analysis presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence. Public lands and waters that were closed are opened, and lease revenues flow to Alaska (50%), local impact aid, and the energy trust fund rather than general revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, coastal communities, and public lands

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to issue 200 reactor permits by 2040 if there are enough applicants, overriding the independent case-by-case licensing process that normally governs reactor safety.

It sharply narrows environmental review: offshore lease sales need no additional environmental analysis beyond the program-wide statement, seismic surveys are categorically excluded, Arctic Refuge leasing is deemed compatible with refuge purposes by statute, and non-leasing alternatives cannot even be analyzed in the required Arctic environmental impact statement.

Judicial review is confined to a 60-day filing window in a single D.C. federal court, with the Secretary's environmental analysis presumed correct unless rebutted by clear and convincing evidence, making it harder for affected communities or conservation groups to challenge decisions.

The coal-to-liquids mandate and repeal of the Section 526 fuel-procurement limit favor a fuel with high carbon emissions, and the Pentagon plant is subject to appropriations that are not provided in the bill.
The bill was referred to six House committees and never advanced, so none of its fiscal, environmental, or tradeoffs were ever examined in a hearing or markup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a genuine national security and energy-security rationale (expanded domestic oil, gas, nuclear, and renewables) with aggressive process shortcuts: pre-approval of a leasing plan, categorical exclusions from environmental review, restricted judicial review, a statutory reactor quota, and a Defense Department coal-to-liquids project. Whether expanded drilling revenue would have been large or reliable enough to fund the renewable auctions is unknown; the bill never received any committee analysis. The environmental-review limits and court restrictions are significant costs the bill imposes on the public without offsetting analysis.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to six House committees and five subcommittees on the day of introduction; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Devin Nunes introduced H.R. 5899 on July 28, 2010, with seven cosponsors: Reps. Paul Ryan of Wisconsin, John Shimkus, Rob Bishop of Utah, Mike Simpson, and others.
The bill was referred to six House committees: Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Transportation and Infrastructure.

Within Transportation and Infrastructure, it was further split among the Aviation, Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, Highways and Transit, Railroads Pipelines and Hazardous Materials, and Water Resources and Environment subcommittees; Armed Services referred it to Strategic Forces, Natural Resources to Energy and Mineral Resources, and no committee took further action.
The bill received no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote in the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and oil shale companies kept existing limits on federal leasing in place, avoiding new competing lease sales; environmental-review requirements and public-land closures the bill would have removed were preserved; and the Pentagon was not committed to a coal-to-liquids program. No bill the sponsor proposed became law from this measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, and oil shale companies

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored and no floor vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape beyond the sponsor's party cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have required lease sales every 270 days, offered at least 75% of unleased offshore acreage, opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and cut or waived environmental reviews and judicial challenges for offshore and refuge leasing. Public lands and waters that were protected would have been opened to commercial drilling.

The bill requires a lease sale of 10 additional oil shale research and development parcels within 180 days and lets the Secretary reduce royalties and fees to encourage production. Public mineral resources would have been offered at reduced cost.

The bill directs the Pentagon to build a coal-to-liquids facility and repeals the federal restriction on buying alternative fuels based on their lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions, opening federal procurement to coal-derived fuel.

The bill mandates 200 new reactor operating permits by 2040, revives the Yucca Mountain waste repository review, and sets up licensing for spent-fuel recycling, removing a key obstacle (waste disposal) that has constrained industry growth.

A reverse-auction mechanism would award trust-fund bonuses to renewable electricity producers, including reserved shares for small and mid-sized facilities, but the fund depends on new fossil-fuel lease revenues.
Alaska receives 50% of federal revenues from Coastal Plain leasing and a capped impact-aid fund ($11 million) supports North Slope communities near the refuge.
